statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) — Suspicious activity reporting requirements?
statutory.answer: Neutral: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements apply to financial institutions and depend on whether a covered institution detected suspicious transactions and had a duty to file a SAR; the facts do not identify any financial institution, SAR obligation, or suspicious-activity determination.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates the Secretary (via regulation) to require a “financial institution” to report “any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation,” and provides related protections (e.g., safe harbor and confidentiality). Element-by-element: (1) Covered actor: § 5318(g) applies to a “financial institution” subject to SAR regulations; the fact pattern describes only an individual (SYN_e1f5cb0d) and their transactions, but does not identify the involved bank/MSB/broker-dealer or any covered institution’s role, so coverage cannot be confirmed. (2) Triggering condition: the duty is tied to a “suspicious transaction” as determined under applicable regulations; while there are multiple ACH/wire/card/cheque transactions (generally $276–$1,309) and a medium risk rating, the facts do not state that any transaction was suspected to involve illegal activity, structuring, fraud, or other violations, nor that any institution formed suspicion. (3) Reporting requirement: § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements depend on regulatory thresholds/timelines and an institution’s filing obligation; the record contains no SAR filing/non-filing facts. Therefore, it cannot be determined from the provided facts whether § 5318(g) applies.
